cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to K.D.L. and S.P.K.
cases.holding: Termination of parental rights requires clear and convincing proof of both the child's best interests and a statutory ground of parental fault, and incarceration alone cannot supply the fault finding.
cases.quote: To terminate a parent's rights, a petitioner must prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that termination is in the child's best interests and that there is parental fault.

relevance.DEC-03: Fixes the evidentiary weight a substantiated agency finding must ultimately carry if the State intends to move from finding to termination.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans are measured against the parental-fault grounds this case enumerates, so plan design drives the later fault analysis.
relevance.OUT-02: This is Nevada's governing two-prong termination test and the anchor authority for any NV TPR entry in the chain.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to J.L.N.
cases.holding: The statutory presumptions favoring termination are rebuttable, and a parent's failure to complete a case plan within six months solely because of incarceration is not a ground for finding failure of parental adjustment.
cases.quote: Compelling reasons demonstrate why termination of parental rights was not in J.L.N.'s best interests.

relevance.ACT-02: Establishes that non-completion of a court-ordered case plan caused by incarceration cannot be converted into parental fault.
relevance.OUT-01: Supplies the 'compelling reasons' analysis that keeps reunification available after the statutory clock has run.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows the record showing required before a court may decline to terminate and close or dismiss on the merits.
relevance.FAIL-01: A published reversal of a district court termination for want of substantial evidence — the model for court correction of agency-driven outcomes.

cases.case_name: Washoe County Department of Social Services v. Kory L.G.
cases.holding: A non-offending parent — one not found to have abused or neglected the child — cannot be compelled to comply with an NRS 432B.560 case plan as a condition of reunification, and the agency's reasonable-efforts duty under NRS 432B.393 runs regardless.
cases.quote: the agency must make reasonable efforts to reunify and preserve the family of the child, with the child's health and safety being a paramount concern

relevance.INP-04: Frames what a court may and may not order an agency or a non-offending parent to do once a dependency referral is opened.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the line between the offending and non-offending parent as the escalation from assessment to case-planning occurs.
relevance.DEC-05: Filing on one parent's conduct does not automatically subject the other parent to the petition's service obligations.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports handling a non-offending parent outside the coercive petition track.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary acceptance of services cannot be made a precondition to the return of a child to a parent never found at fault.
relevance.ACT-02: The leading Nevada statement of the reasonable-efforts and case-plan duty at the dispositional stage.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification with a non-offending parent may not be conditioned on case-plan compliance.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to N.D.O., T.L.O., and T.O.
cases.holding: There is no categorical constitutional right to appointed counsel in a Nevada parental-rights termination proceeding; the right is assessed case by case under Lassiter, and absent that right no ineffective-assistance claim lies.
cases.quote: the right to counsel must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, consistent with the United States Supreme Court's decision in Lassiter v. Department of Social Services.

relevance.OUT-02: Controls whether an indigent Nevada parent facing termination is entitled to appointed counsel and, derivatively, to any ineffective-assistance review.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines the narrow appellate opening for attacking a termination on counsel grounds, and so the limits of court correction on appeal.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to S.M.M.D. and T.A.D.
cases.holding: A tribal-state agreement under 25 U.S.C. § 1919(a) may vest a Nevada district court with subject-matter jurisdiction over an Indian child custody proceeding even where § 1911(a) would otherwise place exclusive jurisdiction in the tribal court.
cases.quote: We therefore uphold the district court's jurisdiction over Raena's relinquishment of parental rights under 25 U.S.C. § 1919

relevance.INP-11: The controlling Nevada authority on when a state court may hear an ICWA case and on the tribal-notice requirements that travel with it.
relevance.OUT-02: Jurisdiction and tribal notice are threshold questions before any Nevada court may terminate rights to an Indian child.

cases.case_name: State, Division of Child & Family Services v. Eighth Judicial District Court
cases.holding: Although child welfare and adoption records are confidential under NRS 432B.280, the exceptions in NRS 432B.290 permit a family court to order DCFS to release identifying information so a child may serve siblings' adoptive parents in a sibling-visitation petition.
cases.quote: We conclude that the family court acted well within its jurisdiction in ordering DCFS to disclose the information for the sole purpose of effecting service.

relevance.FAIL-06: Confidentiality under NRS 432B.280 is not absolute; an agency that refuses all disclosure misstates Nevada law.
relevance.PMC-05: The statutory exceptions in NRS 432B.290 are the lawful route to child-welfare records that the blanket-confidentiality claim obscures.

cases.case_name: Maria L. v. Eighth Judicial District Court
cases.holding: Under NRS Chapter 432B a relative with a special interest in the child must be notified of and involved in the placement plan before the court awards custody to the State, and the district court may not give controlling weight to foster parents' wish to raise the child without contact with the natural family.
cases.quote: the district court gave undue weight to the foster parents' desires to raise N.S. without attachment to her natural family

relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement may not be entered without first honoring the statutory notice and participation rights of interested relatives.
relevance.ACT-04: The leading Nevada statement of the familial-preference requirement in NRS Chapter 432B placement decisions.
relevance.OUT-03: Controls the relative's standing to seek guardianship as a permanency option.
relevance.FAIL-01: Writ relief issued because the district court bypassed the statutory relative-placement process — a template for procedural reversal.

cases.case_name: Mulkern v. Eighth Judicial District Court
cases.holding: The rebuttable presumption in NRS 432B.550(5)(a) that a dependent child's best interest is to be placed with siblings applies even after a sibling has been adopted, because adoption does not defeat the statutory sibling-placement presumption.
cases.quote: the district court is required, under NRS 432B.550(5), to apply the rebuttable sibling presumption in determining Baby Girl W.'s placement.

relevance.ACT-03: Any foster placement decision in Nevada must start from the statutory presumption favoring placement with siblings.
relevance.ACT-04: An adoptive parent of a sibling is a statutorily preferred placement the court must consider.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship & Estate of D.R.G.
cases.holding: The NRS 159.061 parental preference in guardianship applies only after the court finds the parent qualified and suitable, and the preference may be rebutted by parental unfitness or by extraordinary circumstances amounting to serious detriment to the child.
cases.quote: parental preference can be rebutted by showing parental unfitness or other extraordinary circumstances.

relevance.ACT-04: Sets the burden a kin caregiver must meet to displace a parent in a Nevada guardianship.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling Nevada standard for guardianship as a permanency outcome over a parent's objection.

cases.case_name: Rennels v. Rennels
cases.holding: The constitutional presumption in favor of a fit parent's decision applies at the court's initial determination of a nonparent's visitation rights, but once a final visitation decree has entered the parent seeking to modify or terminate it no longer carries that presumption.
cases.quote: the parental presumption applies at the time of the court's initial determination of a nonparent's visitation rights.

relevance.OUT-03: A nonparent's judicially approved contact rights acquire res judicata protection and shape kinship permanency arrangements.

cases.case_name: Birth Mother v. Adoptive Parents
cases.holding: Absent a specific Nevada statute authorizing them, post-adoption contact agreements between a birth parent and adoptive parents are unenforceable, and the adoption decree terminates all rights of the natural parent.
cases.quote: Because this agreement is unenforceable under Nevada law and the adoption decree governs, the birth mother cannot seek relief based on the agreement.

relevance.OUT-02: Warns families and counsel that an open-adoption promise made to secure relinquishment carries no legal force in Nevada.

cases.case_name: Jason S. v. Valley Hospital Medical Center
cases.holding: A parent's substantive due process rights are not violated when a district court appoints a temporary guardian under NRS 159.052 to consent to medically necessary care that the parents refused on religious grounds, subject to notice within 48 hours and a hearing within ten days.
cases.quote: we hold that a parent's substantive due process rights are not violated when the district court awards temporary guardianship of a minor child

relevance.INP-07: Defines the medical provider's lawful route when a clinical encounter reveals a refusal of necessary treatment.
relevance.INP-12: An alternative to protective custody: temporary guardianship limited to the medical decision, with statutory notice and hearing deadlines.
relevance.ACT-05: Temporary guardianship functions as the protective order here, restricting parental decision-making without removing the child.
relevance.ACT-06: The controlling Nevada authority for court-authorized emergency medical care over parental religious objection.

cases.case_name: Clark County Department of Family Services v. Eighth Judicial District Court (Sharp)
cases.holding: NRS 432B.290(4) creates only a limited privilege for the identity of a person who reports suspected child abuse — available when the agency determines disclosure would harm an investigation or endanger a person — and it did not bar the court from ordering DFS to disclose reporter identities to a criminal defendant.
cases.quote: we hold that the district court did not exceed its jurisdiction when it ordered DFS to release the names of the individuals who made the reports at issue

relevance.INP-01: Directly governs whether a mandated reporter's identity stays confidential in Nevada — the answer is qualified, not absolute.
relevance.INP-02: A voluntary reporter's anonymity is a limited privilege the agency must affirmatively invoke and justify.
relevance.INP-03: Controls DFS disclosure of its reports to parties in a related criminal prosecution.
relevance.INP-06: The most recent Nevada authority on hotline-reporter confidentiality under NRS 432B.290(4).
relevance.INP-08: A school employee's report is protected only to the extent the agency makes the required harm determination.
relevance.DEC-03: The underlying report and reporter identity may become discoverable once the matter moves into litigation.
relevance.FAIL-06: Shows the precise boundary of a Nevada agency's lawful nondisclosure, against which a refusal can be tested.
relevance.PMC-03: Defines what a review body can and cannot be told about reporters under NRS 432B.290.
relevance.PMC-05: The 2025 statement of how much of the NRS 432B record stays sealed in Nevada.
relevance.PMC-06: The controlling recent rule an automated records analysis must encode about reporter-identity confidentiality.

cases.case_name: Clark County v. Eighth Judicial District Court (Eggleston)
cases.holding: Qualified immunity and Nevada discretionary-act immunity barred suit against a county social worker who allegedly coerced a parent into signing temporary guardianship papers placing his children with relatives instead of filing a petition.
cases.quote: we consider whether qualified and discretionary-act immunity apply to bar suit against a social worker who allegedly coerced a parent to sign guardianship papers

relevance.INP-05: Describes the informal, non-petition route Nevada caseworkers use when a parent is asked to sign children over to relatives.
relevance.DEC-06: The leading recent Nevada case on the alternative-response path of a 'voluntary' relative placement in lieu of a petition.
relevance.ACT-01: Shows how a voluntary arrangement is negotiated and how little civil exposure the caseworker carries if the parent later claims coercion.
relevance.ACT-04: Temporary guardianship with relatives, obtained outside the petition process, is the placement mechanism at issue.
relevance.FAIL-02: Marks the immunity wall a Nevada parent faces when alleging a coerced, non-judicial removal.
relevance.OUT-03: A guardianship reached this way still produces a kinship placement, with the parent's later challenge sharply limited.

cases.case_name: In re A.T.
cases.holding: NRS 432B.530(2) does not confine a party to admitting or denying the petition's allegations; a district court may properly accept a no-contest plea in a Chapter 432B dependency proceeding without the prosecutor's agreement.
cases.quote: we hold that a district court may properly accept a no-contest plea in this context.

relevance.INP-04: Once a referral becomes a petition, this defines the responsive pleas available to the parent at the first hearing.
relevance.DEC-05: The current Nevada rule on how a dependency petition is answered and resolved without a contested adjudication.
relevance.OUT-05: A no-contest plea carries the same consequences as an admission, foreclosing the dismissal a contested hearing might produce.

cases.case_name: In re N.R.R.
cases.holding: A district court in an NRS Chapter 432B proceeding lacks statutory authority to order the child welfare agency to pay rental assistance to a foster parent; the agency retains broad discretion over the services and supports it funds.
cases.quote: We conclude that the district court lacked statutory authority to order DFS to pay rental assistance to a foster parent.

relevance.INP-09: Shows that judicial oversight of a Nevada child welfare agency does not extend to directing its spending — oversight must come from elsewhere.
relevance.ACT-03: Limits what a court may order an agency to fund in support of a foster placement.
relevance.PMC-06: A structural constraint any accountability model must encode: the Nevada juvenile court cannot order agency expenditures.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to S.A.T.
cases.holding: Terminating parental rights in a private termination action based solely on the parental-fault ground of token efforts to communicate is disfavored, particularly where a protective order restricted the parent's contact.
cases.quote: we now hold that terminating parental rights in a private termination action based solely on the parental-fault ground of token efforts to communicate with the child is disfavored.

relevance.ACT-05: Holds that a protective order restricting contact cannot then be used as the evidence of the parent's token efforts.
relevance.OUT-02: The most recent Nevada limit on the token-efforts ground in privately initiated terminations.
relevance.OUT-05: Affirms denial of a termination petition where the fault grounds were not proven by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: Illustrates appellate enforcement of the clear-and-convincing standard against an unsupported fault finding (by affirmance of a denial, not reversal).

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to R.A.S.
cases.holding: Because no agency reunification services are available in a privately filed termination action, courts must approach private petitions with particular care; here the findings of abandonment and other parental fault were not supported by substantial evidence and the termination was reversed.
cases.quote: In contrast, when a private party petitions to terminate parental rights, no such services are available.

relevance.ACT-02: Draws the sharp line between an agency case with NRS 432B.393 services and a private petition where no services exist.
relevance.OUT-01: Explains why the reunification-services predicate that normally precedes termination is absent in private petitions.
relevance.OUT-02: Current Nevada guidance on the heightened care owed in private terminations, from a Fourth Judicial District (Elko) appeal.
relevance.OUT-05: Reversal for want of substantial evidence, returning the family to an intact status.
relevance.FAIL-01: A 2025 published reversal of a district court termination — the freshest statement of the substantial-evidence review standard.

cases.case_name: Public Employees' Retirement System of Nevada v. Nevada Policy Research Institute, Inc.
cases.holding: Under the Nevada Public Records Act an agency must disclose requested information where producing it merely requires searching an existing database, the information is readily accessible and not confidential, and speculative risks of disclosure do not outweigh the public's interest in access.
cases.quote: is readily accessible and not confidential, and the alleged risks posed by disclosure do not outweigh the benefits of the public's interest in access to the records

relevance.INP-09: Supplies the records mechanism by which outside reviewers obtain the agency data that triggers oversight.
relevance.FAIL-06: The governing Nevada Public Records Act balancing test against which an agency's refusal to release data is measured.
relevance.PMC-02: Establishes the public's right of access to the agency data that audit and financial review depend on.
relevance.PMC-03: Gives a citizen review panel the legal footing to demand the underlying records rather than agency summaries.
relevance.PMC-05: The leading modern Nevada statement that speculative harm does not defeat a public records request.
relevance.PMC-06: Confirms that database queries against existing records are a disclosable public record in Nevada, not a prohibited new compilation.

cases.case_name: Henry A. v. Willden
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Clark County and Nevada foster children stated clearly established substantive due process claims under the 'special relationship' doctrine for inadequate safety and medical care, and the court applied the Blessing test to determine which Child Welfare Act and CAPTA provisions are privately enforceable under § 1983.
cases.quote: Having examined the relevant contours of a foster child's clearly established due process rights to adequate safety and medical care

relevance.INP-07: Foster children have an enforceable due process right to adequate medical, dental and mental health care while in state custody.
relevance.INP-09: A systemic class action against the Nevada and Clark County child welfare agencies — the litigation form that oversight failure takes.
relevance.ACT-03: Placing a child in foster care creates the custodial 'special relationship' that imposes affirmative constitutional duties on Nevada agencies.
relevance.ACT-06: The state's duty to provide medical care, including monitoring of psychotropic medication, attaches on placement.
relevance.OUT-04: The safety and medical-care duties run for the entire period the youth remains in state custody, including extended care.
relevance.OUT-06: Frames agency liability where a child in care suffers serious harm.
relevance.FAIL-03: Applies the Blessing/Suter framework that decides which federal Title IV-E and CAPTA duties a child may actually enforce.
relevance.FAIL-04: The Nevada-specific roadmap for constitutional claims arising from harm to a child under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-01: Shows what federal performance obligations look like when litigated rather than merely reviewed under the CFSR.
relevance.PMC-02: Documents the categories of systemic Nevada agency failure that audit findings typically mirror.
relevance.PMC-03: Identifies the specific Nevada system deficiencies a citizen review panel would be evaluating.
relevance.PMC-04: Identifies the recurring care failures that a fatality-review body is meant to surface before a death occurs.
relevance.PMC-06: The anchor case for any structural analysis of the Nevada and Clark County child welfare systems.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A social worker who removes a child without a warrant violates the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments unless reasonable cause exists to believe the child would suffer serious bodily harm in the time it would take to obtain a warrant.
cases.quote: Officials, including social workers, who remove a child from its home without a warrant must have reasonable cause to believe that the child is likely to experience serious bodily harm

relevance.INP-12: Defines the exigency that must exist before Nevada officials may take protective custody without judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: The operative test for emergency removal: the harm must be likely within the time a warrant would take.
relevance.FAIL-02: The standard a wrongful-removal § 1983 claim in the Ninth Circuit is measured against.

cases.case_name: Mabe v. San Bernardino County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Officials may not enter a home or seize a child without prior judicial authorization unless they possess information at the time of seizure establishing reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury, and the intrusion must be no broader than necessary to avert that injury.
cases.quote: reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury and that the scope of the intrusion is reasonably necessary to avert that specific injury.

relevance.INP-06: A hotline allegation, standing alone, does not supply the reasonable cause required for warrantless entry or seizure.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the constitutional ceiling on what an escalated investigation may do without a court order.
relevance.INP-12: The source of the Ninth Circuit's imminent-danger formulation for warrantless protective custody.
relevance.DEC-01: An uncorroborated allegation that fails this test is one the agency must investigate further rather than act on.
relevance.DEC-02: Accepting a report for investigation does not authorize entry or seizure absent this showing.
relevance.DEC-04: The controlling formulation of both the cause and the scope limits on emergency removal.
relevance.FAIL-02: The foundational Ninth Circuit standard for unlawful warrantless removal and entry.

cases.case_name: Wallis v. Spencer
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Officials who seized children on the basis of a non-existent court order and subjected them to invasive medical examinations without parental notice, consent or judicial authorization violated the family's constitutional rights; any intrusion must be strictly circumscribed by the exigency that justified it.
cases.quote: The right to family association includes the right of parents to make important medical decisions for their children, and of children to have those decisions made by their parents

relevance.INP-03: Police acting on a supposed order without verifying it is the paradigm of an unlawful law-enforcement-driven seizure.
relevance.INP-07: Parents hold the constitutional right to make and be present for their children's medical decisions, including forensic examinations.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody must be strictly limited to what the claimed emergency actually requires.
relevance.DEC-04: A removal justified by exigency is unlawful in scope once it exceeds what the exigency demands.
relevance.ACT-06: Invasive medical or forensic examinations of a seized child require parental notice and consent or judicial authorization.
relevance.FAIL-02: The leading Ninth Circuit case on seizure of children absent a real court order or true exigency.

cases.case_name: Capp v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A social worker who threatens to terminate a parent's custody in retaliation for the parent's protected criticism of the agency violates the First Amendment, and is not entitled to qualified immunity.
cases.quote: A reasonable official would have known that taking the serious step of threatening to terminate a parent's custody of his children

relevance.INP-05: A parent who seeks help or questions the agency may not be punished for doing so.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from screening to investigation driven by retaliatory motive rather than risk is actionable.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision to open or expand an investigation may not be made in retaliation for protected speech.
relevance.DEC-06: A 'voluntary' alternative-response agreement obtained under threat of removal is constitutionally suspect.
relevance.ACT-01: Consent to voluntary services extracted by a threat to remove the children is not genuinely voluntary.
relevance.FAIL-05: The leading Ninth Circuit authority on retaliation by child welfare officials against a parent.

cases.case_name: Mann v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A county violates parents' Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process rights when it performs medical examinations of removed children without notifying the parents and without either parental consent or judicial authorization, and the children's Fourth Amendment rights are separately implicated.
cases.quote: the County violates parents' Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process rights when it performs the Polinsky medical examinations without notifying the parents

relevance.INP-07: Routine intake medical examinations of children entering care are not exempt from parental notice and consent requirements.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency medical or forensic care of a child in protective custody requires consent or a court order absent a genuine emergency.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: The federal constitutional floor that an agency finding must eventually meet if it is to support severance of the parent-child relationship.
relevance.ACT-02: Service-plan compliance evidence must be able to carry a clear-and-convincing burden, not a preponderance.
relevance.OUT-01: Until the State meets that burden, the constitutional presumption favors preserving and restoring the family.
relevance.OUT-02: The controlling federal standard of proof for every termination of parental rights, including Nevada's.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Due process entitles a parent to a hearing on his fitness before his children are taken from him, and a State may not presume unfitness by category.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.INP-12: Emergency custody must be followed promptly by an individualized hearing rather than a categorical presumption.
relevance.DEC-04: Removal before any fitness hearing is constitutionally tolerable only as a genuine emergency measure.
relevance.DEC-05: The petition exists to give the parent the individualized hearing the Constitution requires.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the State cannot prove unfitness at that hearing, the case must end.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Constitution does not require appointed counsel in every parental-rights termination proceeding; whether due process calls for counsel is left to the trial court case by case, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: The federal source of Nevada's case-by-case approach to appointed counsel in termination cases.
relevance.FAIL-01: Counsel determinations are expressly subject to appellate review, supplying one ground for reversal (the Court itself affirmed).

cases.case_name: Troxel v. Granville
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A fit parent's decisions about the care, custody and control of his or her children are presumed to be in the children's best interests, and a court may not override them merely because it would decide differently.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: A parent's own request for help does not waive the presumption that the parent's decisions are in the child's interest (an application of the fit-parent presumption, not language in Troxel).
relevance.DEC-06: Alternative response must respect parental decision-making absent a finding of unfitness.
relevance.ACT-04: Relatives' preferences cannot displace a fit parent's choices about placement and contact.
relevance.OUT-03: The constitutional presumption a nonparent must overcome to obtain guardianship or court-ordered contact.

cases.case_name: M.L.B. v. S.L.J.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on the parent's ability to pay record preparation fees.
cases.quote: just as a State may not block an indigent petty offender's access to an appeal afforded others

relevance.OUT-02: Guarantees an indigent Nevada parent a real appellate remedy from a termination decree.
relevance.FAIL-01: Removes the cost barrier that would otherwise prevent appellate correction of an erroneous termination.

cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Whatever liberty interest foster parents may hold arises from a state-created arrangement rather than intrinsic family rights, and New York's existing pre-removal procedures were constitutionally adequate to protect it.
cases.quote: the procedures provided by New York State in § 392 and by New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect whatever liberty interests appellees may have

relevance.ACT-03: Defines the limited constitutional status of the foster relationship the state creates when it places a child.
relevance.ACT-04: A kin or foster caregiver's interest is weaker than a natural parent's and is shaped by state law, not the Constitution.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a State to protect a child from private violence it did not create, even where the agency received repeated abuse reports and failed to act. (Joshua DeShaney was never in state custody and survived with profound brain injury; this is not a death-in-care case.)
cases.quote: its language cannot fairly be extended to impose an affirmative obligation on the State to ensure that those interests do not come to harm through other means.

relevance.INP-01: A mandated report that the agency receives and does not act on creates no federal constitutional duty to the child.
relevance.INP-02: The same limit applies to third-party reports, which is why state reporting statutes and oversight carry the weight.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out that later proves catastrophic is not, without more, a federal constitutional violation.
relevance.OUT-06: The starting point for analyzing agency responsibility for serious harm to a child, and the reason the custody exceptions matter.
relevance.FAIL-04: The controlling authority limiting § 1983 liability where a child was never taken into state custody.
relevance.PMC-04: The authority limiting liability where the child was never in state custody — which is why administrative fatality and near-fatality review, rather than litigation, is the practical accountability route.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Domicile under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, and children domiciled on the reservation fall within the tribal court's exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) even where the parents voluntarily gave birth off-reservation.
cases.quote: Section 1911(a) establishes exclusive jurisdiction in the tribal courts for proceedings concerning an Indian child

relevance.INP-11: The foundational federal authority on when a state court has no jurisdiction at all over an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's placement scheme, grounded in tribal interests, constrains Nevada's ordinary kinship-preference analysis.
relevance.FAIL-05: Explains that ICWA's preferences rest on tribal political status, not racial classification.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: ICWA is a valid exercise of Congress's Article I authority over Indian affairs, its placement and procedural requirements do not violate the anticommandeering doctrine, and the equal protection and nondelegation challenges failed for lack of standing (so the constitutionality of the placement preferences remains formally open).
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

relevance.INP-11: Confirms that ICWA and its Nevada analogue in NRS Chapter 125E remain fully binding on state courts and agencies.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's placement preferences survive constitutional attack and continue to govern kinship placement of Indian children.
relevance.OUT-02: The § 1912(d) active-efforts and § 1912(f) evidentiary requirements remain enforceable in state termination proceedings.
relevance.FAIL-03: A state's failure to apply ICWA is a failure of binding federal law, not of a waivable federal guideline.
relevance.FAIL-05: Leaves the equal protection challenge to ICWA's preferences undecided for want of standing — a point counsel must not overstate.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Sections 1912(f) and 1912(d) of ICWA do not bar termination of the rights of a parent who never had custody of the Indian child, because there is no 'continued custody' to be broken up and no family to preserve through remedial efforts.
cases.quote: we hold that neither § 1912(f) nor § 1912(d) bars the termination of his parental rights

relevance.INP-11: Narrows which ICWA protections attach when the Indian parent never had physical or legal custody.
relevance.OUT-02: Limits the ICWA active-efforts and heightened-proof requirements in terminations involving a never-custodial parent.
relevance.FAIL-05: Shows the Court construing ICWA narrowly to avoid the equal protection question its preferences would raise.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to L.L.S.
cases.holding: Procedural due process requires that a termination-of-parental-rights trial under NRS Chapter 432B be heard by a district judge in the first instance; a hearing master may not preside, and a district judge's later review of the master's trial record does not cure the defect. The termination order was reversed and the case remanded for a new TPR proceeding.
cases.quote: we hold that due process requires the TPR trial to be heard before a district judge in the first instance

relevance.DEC-05: Marks the line inside a Chapter 432B case: a master may hear the dependency proceeding, but once the matter becomes a TPR trial only a district judge may preside — this materially limits the brief's reliance on master-based procedure.
relevance.OUT-02: Nevada's controlling procedural rule for how a termination must be tried, independent of the sufficiency of the evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: A structural reversal ground: a TPR order produced by a hearing master is vacated on due process grounds even where the record would otherwise support termination, and even where the parent never raised the objection below.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to J.D.N.
cases.holding: The juvenile 'J' file does not automatically form part of the family division's record in a termination proceeding and is admissible only if it satisfies Nevada's evidence rules, including the hearsay rule; NRS 128.090(3) removes only privilege objections, not hearsay objections. A parent who objects to the entire file without identifying the specific hearsay portions waives the objection. Once an NRS 128.109 presumption applies, the parent may rebut it by a preponderance of the evidence. Affirmed.
cases.quote: the "J" file is only admissible if it complies with Nevada's statutes and rules of evidence, including the hearsay rule and any hearsay exception

relevance.INP-01: A mandated reporter's report reaches the termination court inside the 'J' file, and this case holds that it is not automatically in evidence — it must satisfy the hearsay rule like any other document.
relevance.INP-02: Third-party reports compiled into the agency file carry no automatic admissibility in a termination trial.
relevance.INP-03: Law-enforcement referrals and the agency reports built on them are subject to hearsay objection when the State offers the 'J' file.
relevance.INP-06: Hotline intake documents in the 'J' file are admissible only through a hearsay rule or exception, not by virtue of being in the agency's file.
relevance.INP-08: An educator's report travels into court as part of the 'J' file, and this decision governs how that document is tested — by specific objection, portion by portion.
relevance.DEC-03: Tells a parent how a substantiated finding recorded in the agency file can and cannot be used as proof later, and what a lawyer must do to keep the objection alive on appeal.
relevance.ACT-02: Sets the burden for rebutting the NRS 128.109(1) token-efforts and case-plan-noncompliance presumptions that a court-ordered service plan generates: preponderance, not clear and convincing.
relevance.OUT-02: The correct Nevada authority on the evidentiary record in a termination trial; it replaces the mis-citation the earlier draft carried.

cases.case_name: Phillip A. C. v. Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Tribes of Alaska
cases.holding: A tribal enrollment officer's affidavit may be used to establish that a child is an Indian child subject to ICWA, but the adoptive parent must be given an opportunity to rebut it; an Indian tribe has independent standing under 25 U.S.C. § 1914 to challenge a voluntary adoption, and a violation of § 1913(a)'s consent-certification requirement makes the adoption order voidable rather than void. Reversed and remanded so the adoptive parent could present rebuttal evidence.
cases.quote: a Native American tribe has independent standing under the ICWA to challenge the voluntary adoption of a Native American child

relevance.INP-11: Nevada's published answer to two practical ICWA questions the statute does not settle — how Indian-child status is proved in a state court and who may raise ICWA — and it confirms that the tribe can intervene in a voluntary adoption on its own footing.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to N.J.
cases.holding: Abandoning the jurisdictional/dispositional framework of Champagne v. Welfare Division, the court adopted the best-interest/parental-fault standard that Nevada applies today: a district court must find both that termination serves the child's best interest and that parental fault exists. The district court also erred by failing to apply NRS 128.012(2)'s abandonment presumption. Orders reversed and remanded for a new trial.
cases.quote: we now reject our Champagne standard, which requires a district court to find jurisdictional grounds to terminate parental rights before it considers the best interests of the child

relevance.OUT-02: The origin of Nevada's modern two-prong termination test; every later NV TPR case, including K.D.L., traces to this decision.
relevance.DEC-03: Establishes that a fault finding and a best-interest finding are separate inquiries, neither of which a substantiated agency finding supplies by itself.
relevance.ACT-02: Because fault must be independently found, compliance or non-compliance with a court-ordered plan is evidence of fault, not a substitute for it.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal squarely on the ground that the district court applied the wrong legal standard and ignored a statutory presumption.

cases.case_name: Champagne v. Welfare Division of the Nevada State Department of Human Resources
cases.holding: In four consolidated appeals the court held that parental rights may be severed only on clear and convincing proof of parental unsuitability — serious and persistent fault or incapacity, not mere inadequacy — together with dispositional grounds in the child's best interest; it affirmed two terminations and reversed two. Its two-step jurisdictional/dispositional framework was later rejected in In re Parental Rights as to N.J., 116 Nev. 790 (2000), but its unsuitability analysis remains the court's reference point, including in In re Parental Rights as to S.A.T. (2025).
cases.quote: Absent a showing of unsuitability, invasion of the liberty interest in parenthood is not constitutionally warranted.

relevance.OUT-02: The foundational Nevada unsuitability decision; a Nevada TPR brief that omits it reads as incomplete, but it must always be cited with its partial abrogation by N.J. (2000).
relevance.DEC-03: Draws the distinction Nevada still uses between neglect (a condition of the child), unfitness (a condition of the parent) and unsuitability (the constitutional threshold for severance).
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that a parent cannot be found unsuitable for failing to meet case-plan requirements that are unclear, uncommunicated, or impossible to satisfy.
relevance.FAIL-01: Two of the four terminations were reversed for want of clearly and convincingly established unsuitability — the court's model of close appellate scrutiny.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to Q.L.R.
cases.holding: On an issue of first impression, the court held that incarceration resulting from a parent's voluntary criminal conduct does not by itself establish an intent to abandon the child; because the record contained no substantial evidence of abandonment, the termination of the father's parental rights was reversed.
cases.quote: we hold that voluntary conduct resulting in incarceration does not alone establish an intent to abandon a minor child.

relevance.OUT-02: The source of the Nevada incarceration rule that K.D.L. later applies; citing K.D.L. without Q.L.R. cites the derivative rather than the source.
relevance.DEC-03: A parent's imprisonment cannot be treated as a self-proving fault finding.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal for insufficiency: the fault ground the district court relied on was legally unavailable on these facts.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to C.J.M.
cases.holding: Decided as the companion to Q.L.R., this case holds that while incarceration alone cannot justify termination, it is properly weighed with other factors bearing on fitness and the children's best interests; because the district court articulated grounds beyond incarceration — abandonment and more than a year without meaningful contact — termination was affirmed and the agency was not obliged to provide a reunification plan.
cases.quote: incarceration should be considered along with other factors in determining parental fitness and in making a determination on what course of action would serve the children's best interests.

relevance.OUT-02: The other half of Nevada's 2002 incarcerated-parent pair; read with Q.L.R. it shows exactly where the line falls between incarceration as context and incarceration as the ground.
relevance.DEC-03: Fault must be articulated on grounds over and above the fact of imprisonment.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that where the parent's own failure to show interest in the children is the greater cause of the absence of a case plan, the agency was not obligated to provide one.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to D.R.H.
cases.holding: NRS 128.109(2)'s presumption that termination serves the best interest of a child who has lived outside the home for 14 of 20 consecutive months survives strict scrutiny: it is narrowly tailored to the State's compelling interest in permanency, applies only to children removed under NRS Chapter 432B, is rebuttable, and must be read with NRS 128.105's separate fault requirement. Termination affirmed.
cases.quote: We conclude that NRS 128.109(2) is constitutional and that substantial evidence supports the district court's decision to terminate Cristan's and Vincent's parental rights.

relevance.OUT-02: The constitutional answer to a parent who attacks the 14-of-20-month presumption, and the case later decisions cite for Nevada's clear-and-convincing standard.
relevance.DEC-03: Confirms that the statutory presumption supplements, but does not displace, the clear-and-convincing findings of fault and best interest.
relevance.ACT-03: A removal into foster care starts the 14-of-20-month clock that drives this presumption — the single most consequential timing rule for a Nevada family after placement.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to A.J.G.
cases.holding: Neither Nevada nor federal law requires the State to prove that an adoptive placement exists before a court may terminate parental rights, and once the State establishes the NRS 128.109(2) presumption the parent bears the burden of offering evidence of the child's desires under NRS 128.107(2). Termination affirmed.
cases.quote: neither state nor federal law on parental rights termination requires the State to prove the existence of an adoptive placement for a child before a court can terminate parental rights

relevance.OUT-02: Answers the most common parental objection to a Nevada termination petition — that no adoptive home has been identified — and answers it against the parent.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the legal mechanism by which Nevada children become legally free and then remain in care to majority: because no adoptive resource need be proved before rights are severed, a terminated case can end in extended foster care rather than adoption. (The opinion itself says nothing about extended foster care or aging out; the node remains statute-driven.)
relevance.DEC-03: Allocates the evidentiary burden once the agency's presumption attaches, which is where a substantiated case usually turns.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights as to A.D.L. and C.L.B., Jr.
cases.holding: A case plan may not condition compliance on a parent's admission of a criminal act; terminating parental rights because the mother would not admit she intentionally burned her child violated her Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, and once the NRS 128.109(1)-(2) presumptions were rebutted there was no substantial evidence of fault or of best interest. Reversed.
cases.quote: We conclude that a parent cannot be compelled to admit to a crime under the threat of termination of parental rights.

relevance.ACT-02: The clearest Nevada limit on what a court-ordered service plan may demand: it may require treatment and demonstrated safety, but not a confession.
relevance.FAIL-01: A published reversal of a Nevada termination on constitutional grounds, and the strongest Nevada precedent for a parent challenging an admission-based case plan.
relevance.DEC-03: A refusal to admit the agency's substantiated allegation cannot itself be converted into the fault finding.
relevance.OUT-02: Read with Donald B. (2018), it fixes both edges of the rule — no compelled confession, but meaningful therapy can still be required.

cases.case_name: Donald B. v. Nevada Department of Family Services (In re S.L.)
cases.holding: Distinguishing A.D.L., the court held that where termination rested not on the parents' refusal to confess but on years of physical and mental abuse of the oldest child witnessed by the younger children, and on the parents' failure to engage in meaningful therapy or show the insight needed to keep the children safe, there was no Fifth Amendment violation and substantial evidence supported both fault and best interest. Affirmed.
cases.quote: although appellants cannot be compelled to admit to a crime, they can be required to engage in meaningful therapy designed to ensure the children's safety if returned to the home

relevance.ACT-02: Defines what a Nevada case plan may lawfully require of a parent who denies the abuse: meaningful therapy aimed at the children's safety, measured by behavioral change rather than by an admission.
relevance.OUT-02: The counterweight to A.D.L.; a parent cannot use the Fifth Amendment to avoid the treatment component of a plan.
relevance.DEC-03: Shows how a substantiated finding involving one child supports fault as to siblings who witnessed the abuse.

cases.case_name: Destin v. Eighth Judicial District Court (Handwerker-LaMaster)
cases.holding: Once parental rights are terminated, placement is governed by NRS 128.110(2) rather than NRS 432B.550's familial preference; the district court must give due consideration to the agency's placement preference but is not bound by it, because the court retains the duty to decide what placement serves the child's best interest. Writ relief denied; placement with the paternal aunt upheld over the maternal grandmother.
cases.quote: While the district court is not bound by the agency's placement preference, it must give due consideration to that preference in deciding placement.

relevance.ACT-04: The current Nevada statement of how much weight a relative's claim carries against the agency's preference — and it confirms that degree of consanguinity does not control.
relevance.OUT-03: Governs the contest between two willing kin caregivers at the permanency stage, including the court's authority to override the agency.
relevance.OUT-02: Post-termination adoptive placement decisions run through NRS 128.110(2), not the Chapter 432B preferences that applied before termination.

cases.case_name: Public Employees' Retirement System v. Reno Newspapers, Inc.
cases.holding: Under the Public Records Act the agency bears the burden of proving confidentiality, either by identifying a statute that declares the record confidential or by showing its interest in nondisclosure clearly outweighs the public interest; NRS 286.110(3) protects individual members' files but does not protect the same information when it appears in reports generated from those files. Affirmed in part and vacated in part.
cases.quote: The state entity bears the burden of overcoming this presumption of openness by proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the requested records are confidential.

relevance.FAIL-06: The burden-allocation rule a requester uses when an agency simply refuses — silence is not a defense; the agency must prove confidentiality.
relevance.PMC-05: The foundational modern Nevada Public Records Act decision that PERS v. NPRI builds on; it supplies the presumption of openness, the narrow-construction rule and the balancing test.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the point an automated records analysis must encode: aggregated or derived reports are not confidential merely because the underlying individual file is.

cases.case_name: In re Public Records Request to Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department
cases.holding: A government agency cannot obtain an advance judicial ruling on its own disclosure obligations: the Judicial Confirmation Law does not reach LVMPD, which is not a municipality, and NRS 239.0107's mandatory five-business-day response duties foreclose declaratory relief in response to a records request. The court noted that a third party who is the subject of requested records is not similarly barred from a reverse-records action. Affirmed.
cases.quote: the Act does not allow a governmental entity to bypass NRS 239.0107 and seek declaratory relief in response to a public records request

relevance.FAIL-06: Closes the principal delay tactic available to a Nevada agency — it must answer the request within five business days and cite a legal basis for any claimed confidentiality rather than litigate first.
relevance.PMC-05: The most recent Nevada Supreme Court statement on the Public Records Act, decided the same term as Sharp, and the one that fixes the procedural posture of any transparency dispute.

cases.case_name: Eggleston v. Stuart
cases.holding: Following Patsy v. Board of Regents, a plaintiff generally need not exhaust administrative remedies before bringing a § 1983 claim, subject to Zinermon v. Burch's narrow exception for procedural due process claims. Because the father's claim that a caseworker and police coerced him into signing a temporary guardianship was a substantive due process claim, dismissal for failure to exhaust his DFS substantiation appeal was error, as was the ruling that punitive damages were unavailable against the caseworker. Reversed and remanded.
cases.quote: a party generally is not required to exhaust administrative remedies before filing a § 1983 civil rights claim

relevance.FAIL-02: The threshold Nevada holding for a coerced- or unlawful-removal suit: a parent may sue under § 1983 without first finishing the agency's own substantiation appeal.
relevance.ACT-01: The facts are a voluntary-services case that turned coercive — a family that agreed to a DFS program and was then pressed to sign away custody under threat.
relevance.INP-05: Shows the risk a parent runs in self-referring to the agency, and that the remedy for what follows is not confined to the agency's internal process.
relevance.OUT-03: The instrument used was a temporary guardianship to a relative, obtained under threat, which the court treated as the injury rather than as a permanency outcome.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no privately enforceable right: it is enforced through the Secretary's approval and oversight of the state plan, not through § 1983 or an implied cause of action by the children the Act benefits. Seventh Circuit reversed.
cases.quote: neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

relevance.PMC-01: The controlling federal answer to why CFSR-style monitoring is the remedy for state non-performance: the Adoption Act's plan requirements are enforced administratively by HHS, not by the children in court.
relevance.PMC-02: Explains why audit and funding leverage — rather than private litigation — is the operative check on how a state spends Title IV-E money.
relevance.FAIL-03: A state's failure to meet the federal reasonable-efforts standard is a federal compliance problem, not a private cause of action; this is the case Henry A. v. Willden's Blessing/Suter analysis applies.
relevance.ACT-02: Sets the ceiling on what 'reasonable efforts' gives a Nevada parent: it shapes what the agency owes HHS, and a parent's leverage over a service plan comes from NRS 432B.393 and the juvenile court, not from the federal statute.

NO NEVADA CASE LAW EXISTS IN COURTLISTENER ON MANDATORY-REPORTER DUTY OR REPORTER IMMUNITY. Four separate searches of nev and nevapp ('432B.160'/'432B.220' immunity; reporter good-faith immunity; teacher/physician/social-worker failure to report; civil liability for failure to report) returned zero on-point results, and the zero results for '432B.220' and 'mandatory reporter child abuse' were independently confirmed on verification. For INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-07 and INP-08, the operating authority in Nevada is therefore statutory — NRS 432B.220 (duty to report), NRS 432B.160 (immunity for good-faith reports), NRS 432B.240 (criminal penalty for failure to report) — plus the CAPTA floor at 42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116. The cases mapped to those nodes go to what happens to a report once made (Sharp on reporter-identity confidentiality) and to the absence of a federal constitutional remedy for an unacted-upon report (DeShaney). A user should not be told Nevada appellate courts have construed the reporting duty itself; they have not, in the published record available here.

A targeted search for age-of-majority/age-21/independent-living jurisdiction returned zero Nevada results, and the zero result for '432B.594'/'extended foster care' was independently confirmed. OUT-04 is therefore carried by the federal standard — the Chafee Foster Care Independence Act (Pub. L. 106-169) and the Fostering Connections Act (Pub. L. 110-351), with NRS 432B.594 governing Nevada's extended-care program — plus Henry A. v. Willden (safety and medical-care duties run for the duration of state custody). This node is the thinnest in the NV layer and must be flagged as statute-driven.

HAALAND v. BRACKEEN REQUIRES A CAREFUL READ, NOT A SOUNDBITE. Brackeen rejected the equal-protection and nondelegation challenges to ICWA's placement preferences for lack of standing, not on the merits — the constitutionality of the preferences themselves remains formally open and must never be described as settled. This caveat is carried in the published entry as well as in these notes.

NEVADA HAS ITS OWN INDIAN CHILD WELFARE STATUTE, NRS CHAPTER 125E, which independently requires good-faith inquiry, tribal notice, active efforts, qualified expert witnesses and transfer to tribal court. It postdates In re Parental Rights as to S.M.M.D. (2012), and no published Nevada opinion construing NRS Chapter 125E was found in CourtListener. INP-11 accordingly pairs the surviving Nevada ICWA cases with the three controlling federal decisions (Holyfield, Adoptive Couple, Brackeen); practitioners must read NRS Chapter 125E alongside them because it may impose duties the older Nevada cases did not address.

DISTINCTIVELY NEVADA POINTS A PRACTITIONER SHOULD KNOW, all drawn from opinions read here: (a) reasonable efforts under NRS 432B.393 cannot be converted into a case-plan mandate against a NON-OFFENDING parent (Kory L.G.); (b) NRS 432B.550(5)(a) creates a rebuttable presumption favoring SIBLING placement that survives a sibling's adoption (Mulkern); (c) a relative with a 'special interest' under NRS 432B.457(2)(a)(1) must be notified and involved BEFORE custody is awarded to the State (Maria L.); (d) a no-contest plea is available in a Chapter 432B petition without prosecutor agreement (In re A.T.); (e) PRIVATE termination petitions get heightened judicial scrutiny precisely because no agency services exist (R.A.S., S.A.T.); (f) reporter identity is protected only by a LIMITED privilege the agency must invoke and justify (Sharp); (g) a Nevada juvenile court cannot order the agency to spend money on a placement (In re N.R.R.); (h) post-adoption contact agreements are UNENFORCEABLE in Nevada (Birth Mother); (i) a TPR trial must be heard by a district judge in the first instance, never a hearing master (L.L.S.).
